RagShortTexts: In 1259 Crusader states clung to coastal forts, navigating between Mongol terror and Mamluk power.

Variants.Content: In AD 1259, the years between the failure of the Seventh Crusade under Louis IX and the looming Eighth Crusade of 1270 left Outremer a shrinking strip of coast. The kingdom had withered into a string of fortified garrisons anchored at Acre and Tyre, while the county of Tripoli and the principality of Antioch clung to their own defences. Hulagu's Mongols had sacked Baghdad in 1258 and pushed into Syria, and the Mamluk sultanate of Cairo waited on the other side of the desert. Caught between those two powers, the Frankish barons struggled to preserve their maritime footholds. Without a large Western army, every garrison depended on its own walls, its own rations, and the uncertain goodwill of the nearest Muslim ruler.

The barons of Jerusalem and the masters of the Temple and Hospital harbor no illusions of reconquering Holy Zion alone. Preserving our sea walls at Acre, husbanding Italian shipping revenue, and keeping precarious neutrality while Tartars and Saracens butcher one another represents our sole hope of survival.

Between Saracen horse archers and rumours of pagan Mongol riders who pile skulls into mountains, our crossbowmen sleep in mail. Every night the watch hears a rider's hooves on the causeway and thinks of Baghdad. Outremer is no longer a land of glory. It is a butcher's yard, and a single drunken sentry could set it alight.

Frankish lords pray to their saints while our olive groves burn under foreign hooves. When horsemen ride through, it matters little whether they carry cross, crescent, or nine-tailed yak standards—the harvest is trampled all the same.
